title: Search systems
scopeHtml: Scope: inverted index, Elasticsearch/Lucene, relevance, indexing pipelines. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why databases are bad at search
notes.html:
Text search asks "which documents contain these words, best matches first". A relational database with LIKE '%shoes%' has to scan every row, because a B-tree index sorts whole values and cannot help with a middle-of-string match. On 100M product rows that is seconds to minutes per query.

A search system flips the structure so lookup by word is instant, adds language handling (stemming, synonyms, typos) and ranks results by relevance.

Worked example. 50M product titles. SELECT ... WHERE title ILIKE '%running shoes%' scans about 5 GB of text: roughly 5 to 20 s. Elasticsearch on the same data: 10 to 50 ms.

Postgres has basic full-text search (tsvector, GIN index) which is a good first step under a few million documents; it lacks easy distributed scaling, rich relevance tuning and facets.

Industry examples. Amazon and Flipkart product search, GitHub code search, Uber Eats restaurant search, Swiggy dish search, Slack message search; Wikipedia uses Elasticsearch (previously Lucene-based).

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page to find "photosynthesis", you look it up alphabetically and get page numbers.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing LIKE '%x%' or regex for search at scale.
  • Treating the search engine as the primary database of record.

notes.title: The inverted index
notes.html:
An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it (a posting list). Building it is the heart of Lucene, Elasticsearch, Solr and OpenSearch.

Steps (analysis pipeline) for each document:

  1. Tokenize: split text into words. "Red running-shoes!" -> red, running, shoes.
  2. Normalize: lowercase, strip accents, remove punctuation.
  3. Stop words (optional): drop "the", "a" (modern engines often keep them).
  4. Stem or lemmatize: running -> run, shoes -> shoe.
  5. Synonyms (optional): sneakers = shoes.
  6. Store term -> sorted list of (docId, term frequency, positions).
Doc1: "red running shoes"
Doc2: "blue running shirt"
Doc3: "red shirt"

Term     Postings (docId : positions)
red      1:[0]  3:[0]
run      1:[1]  2:[1]
shoe     1:[2]
blue     2:[0]
shirt    2:[2]  3:[1]

Query "red AND shirt": postings(red) = {1,3}, postings(shirt) = {2,3} -> intersect = {3}

Intersection of sorted lists is fast (merge walk, skip lists, bitmaps). Phrase queries use positions ("running shoes" needs run at p and shoe at p+1).

Lucene internals worth knowing.

  • The index is split into immutable segments. New documents go into an in-memory buffer, flushed to a new small segment. Segments are never edited; deletes are marked in a bitset and removed during merges (background compaction of many small segments into fewer big ones).
  • Posting lists are compressed (delta encoding plus bit-packing, frame of reference).
  • A term dictionary uses an FST (finite state transducer) held in memory for prefix lookups.
  • Doc values (column-oriented) support sorting and aggregations; stored fields keep the original _source.

Worked example. 10M docs, vocabulary 2M terms. Posting list for "the" has 9M entries; compressed delta ids at about 1 byte each is about 9 MB. A query for rare term "kubernetes" touches a list of 40k entries, tiny. Cost depends on posting-list length, which is why rare terms are cheap and common terms are expensive.

Decision gravity. Choosing the analyzer is nearly a one-way door: changing it needs a full reindex because tokens are baked into the index at write time. Design analyzers (language, synonyms, edge n-grams for autocomplete) before loading hundreds of millions of documents.

Industry examples. Apache Lucene is the library under Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Solr and (a variant of its ideas) many others; Tantivy (Rust) and Bleve (Go) are Lucene-like; Postgres GIN is an inverted index too.

Everyday analogy. The book index again: word to pages. Building it is expensive once; looking up is cheap forever.

Common interview traps.

  • Using different analyzers at index time and query time and wondering why nothing matches.
  • Thinking updates are in-place; they are delete plus insert of a whole document.
  • Forgetting that stemming changes meaning ("university" vs "universe" in aggressive stemmers).

notes.title: Relevance ranking: TF-IDF and BM25
notes.html:
Finding matching documents is easy; ordering them is where search quality lives.

Intuition:

  • Term frequency (TF): a doc mentioning "shoe" 5 times is more about shoes than one mentioning it once, but with diminishing returns.
  • Inverse document frequency (IDF): rare words matter more. "the" appears everywhere (useless), "gore-tex" is rare (informative).
  • Field length normalization: a match in a 3-word title beats the same match in a 3,000-word description.

BM25 (default in Lucene since version 6 / Elasticsearch 5) refines TF-IDF with saturating TF and length normalization:

score(q,d) = sum over terms t: IDF(t) * (tf * (k1 + 1)) / (tf + k1 * (1 - b + b * len/avglen))

Defaults: k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75. Raising k1 makes repeated terms matter longer; b=0 disables length normalization.

Beyond text score, real search blends many signals:

  • Field boosts: title^3, brand^2, description^1.
  • Business signals: popularity, rating, recency, price, in-stock, personalization.
  • Function score / rescoring: run cheap retrieval for the top 1,000, then rerank the top 100 with an expensive model (learning to rank, LambdaMART, neural cross-encoders).
  • Semantic / vector search: embed queries and docs, find nearest neighbours (HNSW indexes, Elasticsearch dense_vector, OpenSearch k-NN, pgvector), often hybrid with BM25 and merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
{
  "query": {
    "multi_match": {
      "query": "running shoes",
      "fields": ["title^3", "brand^2", "description"],
      "type": "best_fields"
    }
  },
  "size": 20
}

Worked example. Query "shoe". Doc A: title "Shoe" (len 1), doc B: description with 200 words mentioning shoe once. BM25 gives A a much higher score through length normalization even though TF is equal. If doc C is a sponsored, out-of-stock item, a business rule can demote it with a function score multiplier of 0.1.

Measure quality. Offline: NDCG@10, MRR, precision@k against human-labelled judgments. Online: click-through rate, zero-result rate, add-to-cart rate, A/B tests. Debug with explain API.

Industry examples. Amazon's A9 mixes text match with sales rank; Google uses PageRank-like link signals plus ML; Airbnb applies learning-to-rank on top of Elasticsearch; Etsy and Walmart publish talks on hybrid lexical and vector retrieval.

Decision gravity. Ranking formulas are reversible via config and A/B test (cheap to change). Heavy models raise latency; every 10 ms matters. Personalization adds cache fragmentation.

Everyday analogy. A librarian who finds all books containing your word, then puts first those where it is the title, rare, and popular.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "ranking = keyword count".
  • Ignoring evaluation: no judgment set, no A/B test.
  • Putting an expensive model on all matching docs instead of a rerank of top N.

notes.title: Elasticsearch architecture: nodes, shards, replicas
notes.html:
An Elasticsearch cluster is nodes holding shards of indices; each shard is a self-contained Lucene index.

  • Index: a logical collection (like a table), for example products.
  • Primary shard: a horizontal slice of the index (documents routed by hash(_id) % number_of_primary_shards). The primary count is fixed at creation (can be changed only by split/shrink/reindex).
  • Replica shard: a copy of a primary: failover plus extra read capacity.
  • Node roles: master-eligible (cluster state, elections), data (hold shards; tiers hot/warm/cold), ingest (pipelines), coordinating (route and merge).

Query path is scatter-gather in two phases:

  1. Query phase: coordinator sends the query to one copy of every shard; each returns its top from+size doc ids with scores.
  2. Fetch phase: coordinator merges, picks the global top N, then fetches the full documents from the owning shards.
PUT /products
{
  "settings": { "number_of_shards": 6, "number_of_replicas": 1,
                "refresh_interval": "5s" },
  "mappings": { "properties": {
    "title":  { "type": "text", "analyzer": "english" },
    "brand":  { "type": "keyword" },
    "price":  { "type": "float" },
    "created":{ "type": "date" } } }
}

Near real-time. A new document is searchable after a refresh (default every 1 s), not instantly; it is first in memory, flushed to a segment visible for search. Durability comes from the translog (fsync per request by default or per 5 s with async), then periodic flush/commit to disk. Hence "near real-time search", not real-time.

Sizing rules of thumb (confirm in current docs).

  • Aim for shard sizes of 10 to 50 GB (up to about 50 GB for search; logs often 20 to 40 GB).
  • Keep fewer than about 20 shards per GB of heap on a node.
  • Give Elasticsearch heap at most about 50% of RAM and under about 31 GB (compressed object pointers), rest left for the OS page cache that Lucene relies on.
  • Too many tiny shards waste memory; too few big shards limit parallelism and slow recovery.

Cluster health. green = all shards allocated, yellow = replicas missing, red = a primary is missing. Mapping explosion (dynamic fields from user-controlled JSON keys) and unbounded wildcards cause outages.

Deep pagination. from=10000,size=10 makes each shard produce 10,010 hits; the default cap index.max_result_window = 10,000 prevents this. Use search_after with a sort tiebreaker, or point-in-time (PIT) for deep paging.

Worked example. 600 GB of product data, growth 20%/year. Target 30 GB per shard: 20 primaries, 1 replica = 40 shards, 1.2 TB of disk plus 30% headroom = about 1.6 TB across e.g. 4 data nodes of 500 GB usable disk each.

Decision gravity. Primary shard count is hard to change (one-way-ish); overshard slightly using the index lifecycle and rollover for time-based data. Use aliases (products -> products_v7) so you can reindex behind the scenes and switch with no client change.

Industry examples. Netflix, Uber, GitHub (moved code search to its own Rust-based engine), Wikipedia, and countless observability stacks (ELK/Elastic Stack, OpenSearch at AWS). Time-series logs use data streams with rollover at 50 GB or 1 day.

Everyday analogy. A publisher with several print shops, each holding a part of the catalogue; a customer question goes to all shops, each shop sends its best candidates, a manager picks the overall best.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Elasticsearch is ACID or a source of truth.
  • Setting number_of_shards to 100 "for scale".
  • Deep paging with large offsets.
  • Forgetting refresh delay when a test reads right after write.

notes.title: Indexing pipelines: keeping search in sync
notes.html:
The search index is a derived copy of data that lives in a database; you need a reliable pipeline to keep it updated.

Options:

  1. Dual write from the app (write to DB and to ES). Simple but fragile: if the second write fails, they diverge, and ordering is not guaranteed. Avoid.
  2. Transactional outbox: the app writes the row and an event row in one DB transaction; a relay publishes events to a queue. Reliable.
  3. Change data capture (CDC): Debezium reads the Postgres WAL/MySQL binlog and publishes row changes to Kafka; a consumer indexes them into Elasticsearch. No app changes; handles any writer.
  4. Periodic batch reindex from DB snapshot: simplest, high lag; good for the initial load.

Design points:

  • Idempotent upserts: use the DB primary key as document _id and the row version as version_type=external so late or duplicated events never overwrite newer data.
  • Bulk API: send batches of 1,000 to 5,000 docs (5 to 15 MB) rather than one request per doc; during large loads set refresh_interval: -1 and number_of_replicas: 0, then restore.
  • Backpressure and retries with a dead-letter queue for poison documents (mapping errors).
  • Full reindex without downtime: build products_v8 in the background from a snapshot while consuming the change stream into both indexes, verify counts and sample queries, then flip the alias atomically.
  • Deletes: capture tombstones; otherwise deleted products still appear.
  • Denormalization: search docs embed what they need (brand name, category path) because there are no joins; when a brand is renamed, reindex affected docs.
# Atomically switch the alias after a reindex
curl -XPOST localhost:9200/_aliases -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "actions": [
    {"remove": {"index": "products_v7", "alias": "products"}},
    {"add":    {"index": "products_v8", "alias": "products"}}
  ]}'

Worked example. 5,000 product updates/s peak. Bulk size 2,000 docs: 2.5 bulk requests/s, easy. Pipeline lag budget 5 s: monitor consumer lag in Kafka and the refresh delay; if lag exceeds 30 s, alert because search shows stale price.

Industry examples. Debezium + Kafka + Elasticsearch connector is the standard open-source setup; LinkedIn's Galene and Uber's search infra feed from Kafka streams; Shopify and Etsy rebuild indexes via alias swap.

Decision gravity. CDC/outbox gives decoupling and replay (reversible, correct under failure). Dual write is easy now and expensive later. The alias-swap pattern makes mapping changes routine instead of a crisis.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper archive clerk who receives a notice for every change in the main records office and updates the card catalogue; if the clerk misses a notice, the catalogue lies.

Common interview traps.

  • Dual writes without reconciliation.
  • Not planning for reindexing (mapping change = reindex).
  • Forgetting deletes and out-of-order events.
  • Treating the index as authoritative: always able to rebuild from the source of truth.

notes.title: Search features: autocomplete, typos, facets, scaling
notes.html:
Autocomplete. Use edge n-grams at index time (sho, shoe) or a dedicated completion suggester (FST in memory), plus popularity weighting from query logs. Latency target under 50 ms, so debounce on the client (200 to 300 ms) and cache top prefixes in Redis/CDN.

Typo tolerance. Fuzzy matching via edit distance (Levenshtein): fuzziness: AUTO allows 0 edits for 1-2 chars, 1 edit for 3-5 chars, 2 edits above. Also "did you mean" suggesters and phonetic analyzers.

Facets / aggregations (counts by brand, price buckets) come from doc values: terms and range aggregations. High-cardinality aggregations cost memory.

Filters vs queries. Filters (exact, yes/no) are cached and do not affect scoring; use them for category, in-stock, price range. Put them in bool.filter.

{ "query": { "bool": {
    "must":   { "match": { "title": "running shoes" } },
    "filter": [ { "term": { "brand": "nike" } },
                { "range": { "price": { "lte": 5000 } } } ] } },
  "aggs": { "by_brand": { "terms": { "field": "brand" } } } }

Scaling and operations.

  • Read-heavy: add replicas (each replica adds read capacity and memory need).
  • Write-heavy: more primaries / faster disks (NVMe), bulk indexing, larger refresh intervals.
  • Hot-warm-cold tiers for time-series data; searchable snapshots to object storage for cold data.
  • Protect the cluster: circuit breakers, query timeouts, limit wildcard/regex/script queries, rate limit per tenant.
  • Monitor: query latency p99, rejected thread pool tasks (search, write queues), JVM heap and GC, segment count, pending tasks, disk watermarks (85% low, 90% high, 95% flood stage by default).

Worked example. Black Friday traffic 20x: 500 -> 10,000 queries/s. Each node does about 1,500 queries/s on this index with p99 under 80 ms. Need 7 data nodes holding replicas; with 6 primaries x 1 replica on 4 nodes, raise replicas to 3 (4 copies) and add 4 nodes, plus a cache for the top 1,000 popular queries which absorbs roughly 40% of traffic.

Industry examples. Amazon and Swiggy autocomplete from query logs, GitHub's custom code-search engine, Algolia / Typesense / Meilisearch as managed or lightweight alternatives, Vespa for large-scale ranking, Google and Bing at web scale.

Decision gravity. Managed (OpenSearch Service, Elastic Cloud, Algolia) vs self-hosted: operations cost vs control and bill; reversible but migrations need reindex. Choose Postgres full-text first if data is small and requirements simple.

Everyday analogy. A shop assistant who guesses your word as you start spelling it, forgives your spelling, and shows filters for size and colour.

Common interview traps.

  • Using expensive wildcard queries (*foo*) in production.
  • Forgetting to cache popular queries and autocomplete.
  • Not isolating the search cluster from the main database failures.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Databases cannot do text search at scale; inverted indexes map terms to posting lists.
  • The analyzer (tokenize, normalize, stem, synonyms) must match at index and query time; changing it means reindexing.
  • BM25 ranks by term frequency, rarity and length; production ranking adds boosts, business signals, learning-to-rank and vectors with hybrid retrieval.
  • Elasticsearch = shards (Lucene indexes) plus replicas, scatter-gather queries, near real-time refresh; size shards 10 to 50 GB and use aliases.
  • Keep the index in sync with CDC or outbox, idempotent bulk upserts, and alias swaps for reindexing; the DB stays the source of truth.
  • Add autocomplete, fuzziness, filters, caching and monitoring for production quality.
